title: Cialledda
author: Marco Bellini
desc: Basilicata's own bread salad, softening stale bread with water before tossing with ripe tomatoes, cucumber, onion, and oregano — a cousin to Tuscany's panzanella from Italy's south.
longDesc: Cialledda differs from panzanella mainly in its bread preparation, softened directly with water rather than soaked in the salad's own juices, resulting in a slightly different texture while sharing the same frugal, resourceful spirit.
ingredients: 300 g (10.5 oz) stale rustic bread, torn into chunks
80 ml (⅓ cup) extra virgin olive oil
steps: Lightly moisten the torn bread chunks with a splash of cold water, just enough to soften without turning soggy, then let sit for a few minutes.
Soak the red onion slices briefly in cold water to mellow their sharpness, then drain.
Squeeze any excess water from the bread and place in a large bowl.
Add the tomatoes, cucumber, onion, and oregano.
Whisk together the olive oil and vinegar, season, and pour over the salad.
Toss well and let sit for at least 15 minutes before serving to let the flavors meld.
Toss once more and adjust seasoning just before serving.
chefTips: Moisten the bread lightly and gradually — it's much easier to add more water than to fix bread that's become mushy.
Genuinely stale, sturdy bread holds up far better than fresh, soft bread.
The ripest, most flavorful tomatoes available make the biggest difference in this simple dish.
commonMistakes: Oversoaking the bread, turning it into an unpleasant mush.
Using underripe, flavorless tomatoes, which this simple dish depends on entirely.
Serving immediately without letting the salad rest and the flavors meld.
storage: Best eaten the day it's made.
reheating: Not applicable; served at room temperature.
healthBenefits: A naturally vegan dish rich in vitamins from the fresh vegetables.
culturalNote: Cialledda reflects Basilicata's frugal cucina povera tradition, transforming humble stale bread into a refreshing dish, much like its better-known Tuscan cousin, panzanella.
